info.title: NGP VAN API (community OpenAPI spec)
info.description:
Community-maintained OpenAPI spec for the NGP VAN API, reverse-engineered from https://docs.ngpvan.com, the NGPVAN/van-cli source, and live probing of the sandbox API. The spec describes the API's actual behavior as observed. Where that behavior deviates from the official docs, the comparison is recorded out of band in `x-docs-discrepancy` fields (hidden by most documentation renderers) and summarized in [DISCREPANCIES.md](https://github.com/NickCrews/van-openapi/blob/main/DISCREPANCIES.md); research evidence and confidence notes live in `x-provenance` fields.

Source repository: https://github.com/NickCrews/van-openapi — file issues and corrections there. This spec is not published or endorsed by NGP VAN; for questions about the API itself, contact APIDevelopers@ngpvan.com.

See [STATUS.md](https://github.com/NickCrews/van-openapi/blob/main/STATUS.md) for per-endpoint research status.

**The API is not callable from a browser.** Its CORS support is incomplete: `api.securevan.com` answers the preflight correctly — reflecting the request origin and allowing the `Authorization` header — but omits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` from the actual response (observed 2026-08-03; a `200` comes back with no `access-control-*` headers at all). A browser therefore sends the request, receives the response, and then blocks the page from reading it. `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is missing as well, which Basic auth would separately require. This affects only browser-based callers; server-side clients such as cURL, Python, or Apps Script are unaffected, since CORS is enforced by the browser rather than the server.

get.summary: Get a person by VAN id
get.description: Retrieves a person record. Related collections (emails, phones, addresses, …) are null unless requested via $expand, and empty arrays when expanded but absent. An unknown, zero, or negative vanId returns the standard 404 error envelope; a non-integer path segment does not match the route and returns an HTML 404 page instead.

parameters.name: vanId
parameters.description: VAN id of the person.
parameters.x-docs-discrepancy: Official docs type this path parameter as string (default "100476252"); the route only matches integers — a non-integer segment returns an IIS HTML 404 page (observed 2026-08-03).

parameters.name: $expand
parameters.description: Related sections to include, comma-delimited eg 'addresses,emails'. Anything outside this set returns 400 INVALID_PARAMETER with a hint listing the valid values. Two sections in the set are still refused in a My Campaign context: `scores` with 403 FORBIDDEN and `pollingLocation` with 400 BAD_REQUEST.
parameters.x-docs-discrepancy: Official docs list only 10 valid $expand values; the API's own INVALID_PARAMETER hint (observed 2026-08-03) lists these 23.

200.description: The person record. Clients that follow redirects can also land here with `text/html` instead: a path segment containing `<`, `>`, `*` or `&` is bounced to the web application's error page, which answers 200 with HTML (see the 302 response).

post.description:
Merges the payload into an existing person record, addressed by id — no matching, no minimum-criteria threshold, and no chance of writing to the wrong duplicate. **This is the endpoint to write through once you have identified a person yourself** (e.g. from GET /people); POST /people/findOrCreate resolves ambiguity silently and creates duplicates below the match threshold.

Fields left out of the body keep their current values, and `emails`, `phones` and `addresses` are appended to what is already there rather than replacing it — there is no way to remove a contact method through this endpoint. The append is idempotent for an identical value: re-sending an email address the person already has — in a later update or twice in one body — does not create a second entry (observed via $expand=emails, 2026-08-08).

Outcomes:

- **The vanId exists** — **302 Found** with a `Location` header pointing back at `/people/{vanId}` and a match-stub body: the same shape POST /people/find returns, **not** the updated person.
- **The body is empty (`{}`)** — accepted, answered the same **302**, and nothing changes.
- **An unknown, zero or negative vanId** — **404**.

x-provenance.note: Merge semantics confirmed by updating only middleName on a person and observing firstName, lastName and employer survive; append semantics by adding a second email and seeing both returned, with isPreferred moving to the newer one. Not in the official docs' page index; the path comes from van-cli (people.ts update), which notes PUT is not supported.

200.description:
Never sent by this endpoint. This is where a redirect-following client *lands* after a successful update:

```
POST /people/102714580         {"firstName": "Cre", …}
  ← 302 Found
    Location: https://api.securevan.com/v4/people/102714580   (same URL)
    {"vanId": 102714580, "status": "Matched"}

GET /people/102714580          ← client re-issues the request at Location
  ← 200 OK
    { the merged person record — the body documented here }
```

A happy accident: the update itself never returns the person, but the followed GET does, so redirect-following clients get the merged result for free. See POST /people/find for the full redirect-following notes, including the `curl -X POST -L` gotcha.

The other way to reach a 200 is a failure: when the 302 was the ASP.NET request-validation bounce (a path segment containing `<`, `>`, `*` or `&`), following it lands on the web application's HTML error page, which answers 200 with `text/html`. Check the content type before parsing JSON.

x-provenance.note: Chain observed end to end with httpx: POST /people/{vanId} with an empty body → 302 back to the same URL → GET → 200 with the full person record.

302.description:
The person was updated. `Location` points back at the person resource; the body is a match stub, not the updated person.

The same status also covers a failure that never reaches the API: a path segment containing `<`, `>`, `*` or `&` is rejected by ASP.NET request validation and redirected to `/Error.aspx?EID={code}` with an HTML body. Check the content type to tell them apart.

get.description:
Searches for people matching the given criteria and returns full person records in the standard pagination envelope. At least one search parameter must be set: firstName, lastName, middleName, streetAddress, city, stateOrProvince, zipOrPostalCode, phoneNumber, email, commonName, or officialName. A request with none of these — even one with filter or paging parameters set — returns 400 INVALID_PARAMETER with the text "This endpoint requires at least one search parameter to be set." Text criteria are case-insensitive prefix matches: lastName=Testpers matches "Testperson", lastName=estperson does not. Related collections on the returned person records are null unless requested via $expand.

**This is the endpoint to use when you only have loose criteria.** Unlike POST /people/find and POST /people/findOrCreate — which refuse to attempt a match until you supply one of a handful of minimum field combinations, and answer Unmatched (or create a duplicate) when you cannot — this search has no such threshold. A single name is a perfectly valid query. In exchange it makes no identity claim: it hands back every person whose fields start with what you typed, and deciding which one is your person, or that none of them is, is your job. Inspect the candidates (with $expand for addresses, emails and phones if you need them) and take the vanId from there.

parameters.name: streetAddress
parameters.description:
Street address, matched as a case-insensitive prefix — but only against the person's **Voting (home) address**, as are `city`, `stateOrProvince` and `zipOrPostalCode`. All four read the single address VAN files as Voting; Work and Custom addresses are not indexed at all, and a Mailing address is only reachable when the person has no separate Voting address (VAN then serves the mailing one under both types, and it becomes findable). So a person can hold an address and still not be findable by it.

The comparison also runs against the *standardized* form VAN stored rather than the text that was written: a person created with `1000 W 5th Ave` is found by `1000 5Th Ave Mall` and **not** by `1000 W 5th Ave`.

POST /people/find has neither limitation — it matches every address type, including the Work and Custom addresses that $expand=addresses never shows.

x-provenance.note: Probed on a person carrying four addresses (Home, Work, Mailing, Custom): only the Home/Voting one was findable here, and only under its standardized form, while POST /people/find matched all four. Calibrated while re-testing what PUT /people/{vanId}/mergeInto does to addresses, where this parameter had been used as an instrument and produced a false negative. Re-probed 2026-08-06 with single-address people: a Mailing-only person reads back with that address listed under both Voting and Mailing (same addressId) and is findable by streetAddress/city/state/zip; a Work-only person is findable by none of them.

parameters.name: city
parameters.description: City, matched as a case-insensitive prefix (`anchor` finds Anchorage; `nchorage` finds nothing). Like `streetAddress`, it reads the **Voting (home) address only** — a person whose mailing or work address sits in a different city is not returned for that city — and it compares against the city VAN standardized at write time, which is not always the one that was written.

x-provenance.note: Probe person with Voting=Anchorage AK, Mailing=Seattle WA, Work=Portland OR, Custom=Sacramento CA: found by Anchorage only. Prefix and case behavior probed with anchor/ANCHORAGE/nchorage.

parameters.name: stateOrProvince
parameters.description: State or province, as the two/three character code — case-insensitive but **not** a prefix match and not the spelled-out name: `AK` and `ak` match, `A` and `Alaska` return nothing. Like `streetAddress`, it reads the **Voting (home) address only**.

x-provenance.note: Same four-address probe person (Voting AK, Mailing WA, Work OR, Custom CA): found by AK/ak only; WA, OR, CA, A and Alaska all returned 0.

parameters.name: zipOrPostalCode
parameters.description:
ZIP or postal code. Like `streetAddress`, this matches the **Voting (home) address only** — a person whose mailing address sits in a different ZIP is not returned for that ZIP.

The value is validated as a postal code (`995` and `995012357` both return 400 INVALID_PARAMETER "is not a valid Postal Code for UsaAndInternational"), and only the 5-digit form matches: a person whose stored ZIP is `99501-2357` is found by `99501` and not by `99501-2357`, which is accepted but returns nothing.

x-provenance.note: The four-address probe person was found by its home ZIP 99501 and not by its mailing ZIP 99503; re-probed with Voting 99501 / Mailing 98101 / Work 97201 / Custom 95814 to the same effect. ZIP+4 and unpunctuated-9-digit forms tested against a person whose address standardized to 99501-2357.

parameters.name: phoneNumber
parameters.description:
Phone number. **Send bare 10 digits — `9072223333`.** Anything else silently finds nothing: the comparison is against the stored 10-digit string, so `(907) 222-3333`, `907-222-3333` and the `1`-prefixed `19072223333` are all *accepted* and then match no one. (Validation is laxer than matching: non-numeric characters are stripped before the value is checked against `^1?[2-9][0-8]\d[2-9]\d{6,6}$`, which is why the formatted forms get through. Failing that regex returns 400 INVALID_PARAMETER with it in the hint.)

This checks **one number per person**: the number VAN flags `isBest` (the first entry `$expand=phones` returns). A person holding home, work, cell and fax numbers is findable only by whichever one is best — for that person the cell — even though the others are on the person record and POST /people/find matches them. A person can also have **no** best number — when every number on it is a work, other or fax number and none was written `isPreferred` — and such a person cannot be found through this parameter at all. See `PersonPhone.isBest` for how the best number is picked.

x-provenance.note: Person with four phones (H 9072223333, W 9073334444, C 9074445555, F 9075556666): only 9074445555 — the isBest/cell one — was findable. Confirmed on three further people that the isBest phone is always the matching one, including a home-only person (isBest home, findable) and a cell+explicitly-preferred-home person (findable by the home number, not the cell). isPreferred is not required: the four-phone person had no preferred phone. The no-best case was probed 2026-08-06: work-only, other-only and Personal/fax-only people each returned an empty items array for their own number, while an otherwise identical work-only person whose number was written with isPreferred:true was found.

post.summary: Find a person matching the given criteria
post.description:
Attempts to match a person in the database. Read-only: never creates person records (use POST /people/findOrCreate for that).

Outcomes:

- **The body supplies a `vanId` that exists** — that person is returned as a **302** and every other criterion is ignored, no threshold involved.
- **One person record matches** — **302 Found**, with a `Location` header pointing at `/people/{vanId}` and a small match-stub body, `{"vanId": …, "status": "Matched"}`.
- **Several person records match** — still a **302** for exactly one of them, and nothing in the response says the match was ambiguous. Which one you get depends on the shape of the criteria; see **When more than one person record matches** below.
- **Nothing matches** — **404** with `{"vanId": null, "status": "Unmatched"}` (a match stub, not the standard error envelope).
- **The criteria fall short of the minimum combination** — **404 Unmatched** as well, not a 400, and indistinguishable from a genuine no-match. This is the common case to guard against; see **The criteria must reach a minimum combination** below.

## The criteria must reach a minimum combination

This endpoint is deliberately conservative — it would rather return nothing than return the wrong person. It does not attempt a match at all until the criteria reach one of these combinations:

- first name + last name + **email address**
- first name + last name + **phone**
- first name + last name + **zip5** + **date of birth**
- first name + last name + **street number + street name + zip5**
- **email address** on its own (a **phone** on its own matches too, though the docs list only email)

Anything short of that — a name on its own, name + date of birth, name + zip — comes back **404 Unmatched** regardless of who is in the database.

**A 404 here does not mean the person does not exist.** It usually means you did not supply enough to identify them. Do not treat Unmatched as "not in the database", and in particular do not follow it with a create — see POST /people/findOrCreate, which silently creates a duplicate for exactly this reason.

**If all you have is a name, use GET /people instead.** That endpoint is a loose prefix search with no threshold: `GET /people?firstName=Harriet&lastName=Kowalski` returns full person records for every candidate, and you decide which one (if any) is your person by inspecting them. Use /people/find only once you hold a strong identifier.

## How the criteria are compared

- Everything you send must agree with the person record. Adding a **wrong** first name to a correct email turns a match into Unmatched — extra criteria narrow, they never widen.
- Comparison is case- and format-insensitive: `HARRIET.KOWALSKI@EXAMPLE.COM` matches the stored lowercase address, `907-555-4242` matches the stored `9075554242`, and per the docs it is accent-insensitive too ("Pérez" matches "Perez"). Names may match on nicknames and variants unless the context has "Disable Partial Matching" turned on.
- The address combination needs the street **number**: `742 Evergreen Terrace` + zip matched; `Evergreen Terrace` + the same zip did not. A wrong zip with a right street also fails.

## When more than one person record matches

Duplicates are common in VAN databases, and this endpoint does not warn you about them: **it returns exactly one vanId with no indication that others also matched.** A 302 is not proof that the match was unique.

The pick is deterministic, but the tiebreak depends on the shape of the criteria — with three identical person records (102719047 < 102719048 < 102720144, same name, email and phone):

- criteria **including a name** (name+email, name+phone, name+dob+zip) → always the **lowest vanId**, i.e. the oldest person record
- criteria **without a name** (email alone, phone alone) → always the **highest vanId**, i.e. the newest person record

It is not the best-matching person record and not the most recently updated one: enriching the newer duplicate so it matched the criteria at least as fully did not move a name-based match off the oldest person record, and touching either duplicate changed nothing.

The consequence to plan for: at the threshold you may be handed a stale or partial duplicate, and a follow-up write through POST /people/{vanId} then lands on whichever duplicate won the tiebreak while the other keeps drifting. When it matters that you have *the* person record rather than *a* person record, list the candidates with GET /people and reconcile them yourself.

Sandbox probing (2026-08-03) shows 302 + Location on match and 404 with a match stub on no match; no 400 was observed even for sparse criteria like firstName-only. Criteria below the documented minimum combinations are also answered 404 Unmatched rather than rejected, so under-specified requests are indistinguishable from genuine no-matches. The docs are also silent on ambiguous matches: when several person records satisfy the criteria the API returns one of them with no indication that others matched.

200.description:
Never sent by this endpoint. This is where a redirect-following client *lands* on a match:

```
POST /people/find              {"firstName": "Ada", "lastName": "Testperson", …}
  ← 302 Found
    Location: https://api.securevan.com/v4/people/102714507
    {"vanId": 102714507, "status": "Matched"}

GET /people/102714507          ← client re-issues the request at Location
  ← 200 OK
    { full person record — the body documented here }
```

requests, httpx, fetch and `curl -L` all follow that redirect and downgrade POST to GET by default, so a match reaches your code as this 200 and a full `Person`, never as the 302 and its two-field match stub. The no-match 404 is not a redirect, so the practical test is `resp.status_code == 200` vs `404`, not `302` vs `404`. The follow-up GET has no `$expand`, so its related collections come back null — re-fetch through the `getMatchedPerson` link if you need addresses, phones or emails.

Gotcha: `curl -X POST -L` keeps the method across the redirect and re-POSTs to `/people/{vanId}` — the *update* endpoint — where IIS answers `411 Length Required` because the re-issued request carries no body. Drop the explicit `-X POST` (`-d` already implies POST) and curl downgrades to GET like everything else.

x-provenance.note: Chain observed end to end with httpx and requests (both: 302 → GET → 200 Person) and with curl 8.7.1 both ways (`-d` alone → GET → 200; `-X POST -L` → POST /people/{vanId} → 411). Documented alongside the raw 302 so both redirect-following clients and raw clients (including the schemathesis fuzzer) conform to this spec.

post.summary: Find a person, or create one if nothing matches
post.description:
Runs the same match as POST /people/find and, when nothing matches, stores the payload as a new person record.

Outcomes:

- **The body supplies a `vanId` that exists** — the match is short-circuited, that person is returned as **302 Found**, and nothing is created.
- **One person record matches** — **302 Found**, with a `Location` header and `{"vanId": …, "status": "Matched"}`.
- **Several person records match** — still a **302** for exactly one of them, with nothing in the response to say the match was ambiguous. See POST /people/find for which one you get.
- **Nothing matches** — **201 Created** with `{"vanId": …, "status": "UnmatchedStored"}`, and the payload is stored as a new person record. Unlike find, this never returns 404 — the no-match case is the create case.
- **The criteria fall short of the minimum combination** — **201 Created** as well: a brand-new person record, even when the person is already in the database. This is the duplicate trap; see **The match half has a minimum threshold** below.
- **The body is empty (`{}`)** — every field is optional, including the name, so this is a no-match: **201** and a blank person record is created.

## The match half has a minimum threshold — below it, you create duplicates

The match runs under the same rules as POST /people/find: nothing is searched until the payload reaches one of these combinations:

- first name + last name + **email address**
- first name + last name + **phone**
- first name + last name + **zip5** + **date of birth**
- first name + last name + **street number + street name + zip5**
- **email address** on its own (a **phone** on its own works too)

**Below the threshold there is no "unmatched" to inspect — the API just creates a second person record.** Posting `{"firstName": "Harriet", "lastName": "Kowalski"}` for a person who is already in the database returns 201 with a fresh vanId, and the two person records now both exist. This is the main way duplicate person records get into a VAN database through the API.

So: only send a payload here that carries a strong identifier. If all you have is a name, search with GET /people first, decide for yourself whether a candidate is your person, and update it by id through POST /people/{vanId} instead.

put.description:
Merges the **secondary** person named in the path into the **primary** person named in the body. The secondary is deleted; the primary survives and keeps its own vanId.

> **Merges are permanent and cannot be undone.** There is no API to reverse one. Afterwards `GET /people/{secondaryVanId}` answers 404 and the id can never be used again. Send `?whatIf=true` first to find out whether a pair is mergeable — but read the warning on that parameter, because only the literal value `true` simulates.

**What happens to the data**, observed on pairs built with conflicting values on both sides:

- Scalar fields the two people disagree on keep the **primary's** value (`firstName`, `sex`, `dateOfBirth`…) — the same defaults the Contacts Merge Wizard applies in the UI.
- Scalar fields the primary left empty are **filled in from the secondary** (`middleName`, `party`, `employer`, `occupation`…), so the primary can come out of a merge holding more data than it went in with.
- `emails`, `phones` and `addresses` are all **combined**, and exact duplicates are collapsed rather than doubled:
  - **Emails** dedupe case-insensitively and regardless of `type`. The primary's copy is the one kept, so its `type` is what survives.
  - **Phones** dedupe on the normalized number — formatting and a leading `1` are ignored — but only within the same `phoneType`. The same number held once as `Personal` and once as `Work` stays as two entries.
  - **Addresses** are combined too, but you will usually not be able to see it. `$expand=addresses` only ever surfaces the best Voting and the best Mailing address, and the primary's own address takes both slots whenever it has one, so a merged-in address is masked rather than missing — `POST /people/find` still matches it. Whether identical addresses are deduped cannot be determined through the API.
- **Notes move to the primary**, keeping their `noteId`.
- The primary inherits the secondary's reachability: `POST /people/find` with an email, phone or address that belonged only to the secondary now resolves to the primary's vanId.

**The preferred email follows the ordinary rule, not a merge-specific one.** The two sets of addresses are pooled and the newest address in the combined set carries the flag — so the primary loses its preferred address whenever the secondary brings in a more recently added one. The exception is an address pinned by an explicit `isPreferred: true` write, which keeps the flag even against a newer incoming address. Phones are unaffected: they only ever take the flag from an explicit write, and where both people had one the primary's survived. Phone ordering after a merge is not stable enough to rely on.

To keep a secondary value the primary overwrote, read both people before merging and write the value back with `POST /people/{vanId}` afterwards.

**Merged-away ids are remembered, but only here.** A vanId that has been merged away is refused on either side of any later merge with `One or more of these contacts has already been merged.` — a different message from the one an id that never existed gets. `GET /people/{vanId}` does not expose that distinction: both simply answer 404. So this endpoint, called with `?whatIf=true`, is the only way to tell a merged-away vanId from one that never existed.

Outcomes:

- **Both ids exist, share a `contactMode`, and neither has been merged before** — **200** with the primary's vanId and a `Location` header pointing at it.
- **Anything else** — **400** with the reason in `text`. Unknown ids are a **400**, not a 404; this endpoint never returns a JSON 404.
- **A secondary equal to the primary** — **500**.

400.description:
The merge was refused, with the reason in `text`. This is the endpoint's catch-all failure status: it covers unknown ids, which are **not** answered 404.

Refusals observed live:

| `text` | Cause |
|---|---|
| `You must have access to both contacts to merge them.` | Either id does not exist, or is outside the key's committee. |
| `One or more of these contacts has already been merged.` | Either id was merged away by an earlier call. Permanent, and applies whichever side the id is on. |
| `Must specify VanIDs for merging` | The body is missing `vanId`, or it is null, `0`, or too large for `int32`. |
| `The body of the request is null or cannot be parsed.` | No body, or a body that is not a JSON object. |
| `VANID {a} and VANID {b} cannot be be merged as they are not the same type of Contact…` | One contact is a person and the other an organization. (The doubled "be be" is the API's own wording.) |

`?whatIf=` with an empty value is also rejected here, with the generic `BAD_REQUEST` / `The request is invalid.`

get.description:
Returns the person's notes in the standard pagination envelope.

View-restricted notes are withheld from API keys: a note saved with `isViewRestricted: true` is absent from `items` and is not counted in `count`, so every note in the response has `isViewRestricted` false. `contactHistory` is always null, even for a note created with one, and `$expand=noteDetails` — the only value the parameter accepts — returns a byte-identical body.

Items come back oldest first by `createdDate`, ties broken by descending `noteId`. `$orderby` is validated against its two allowed properties but has no observable effect: `CreatedDate desc` returns the same order as the default.

An unknown, zero or negative vanId returns the standard 404 envelope; a non-integer path segment matches no route and returns an HTML 404 page.

parameters.name: vanId
parameters.description: VAN id of the person.
parameters.x-docs-discrepancy: Official docs type this path parameter as string (default "100476252"); the route only matches integers — a non-integer segment returns an IIS HTML 404 page (observed 2026-08-04).

parameters.name: $top
parameters.description: Limits the number of results. Default 25, maximum 50. A value of 0 or less returns 400; so does a non-numeric value, with the same message as an over-maximum one.

parameters.name: $skip
parameters.description: Number of results to skip. Must be 0 or greater.

parameters.name: $orderby
parameters.description: Accepted but ignored. The API validates the value — only `CreatedDate` and `IsPinned` pass, case-insensitively, optionally followed by ` desc` — and then returns the default order regardless, including for `desc`.

x-provenance.note: Valid values come from the API's own INVALID_PARAMETER hint on `$orderby=noteId`. All four accepted values, plus `createddate` in lower case, returned an identical item order on a person with six notes.

parameters.name: $expand
parameters.description: `noteDetails` is the only value the API accepts; anything else returns 400 INVALID_PARAMETER with a hint saying so. Expanding has no observable effect — the response is identical with and without it, `contactHistory` included.

200.description: A paginated list of the person's notes.

post.summary: Add a note to a person
post.description:
Creates a note on the person.

On success the response is **204 No Content** with an empty body: the new `noteId` is not returned and there is no `Location` header, so the only way to learn it is to read the notes back. Two notes with identical text are two separate notes — the endpoint is not idempotent.

`isPinned` is accepted and ignored; notes always read back `isPinned: false`. Unknown fields are ignored too. A `contactHistory` object records a Contact History entry alongside the note, but the note's own `contactHistory` stays null in every response.

A note saved with `isViewRestricted: true` can be written but never read back through the API — it is excluded from `GET /people/{vanId}/notes` and from `$expand=notes` on the person.

put.description:
Updates an existing note. Only `text`, `isViewRestricted` and `category` can be changed; `isPinned` and the note's contact history cannot.

**This action is restricted for the key used to research this spec.** Every request returns 403 FORBIDDEN "Access to this action is restricted", whether or not the note exists, so the success path has not been observed live — the request body and the 204 below come from the official docs. `GET` and `DELETE` on this same path are restricted the same way; they are left out of this spec because their success shapes are unknown and undocumented.

The 204 success response is from https://docs.ngpvan.com/reference/peoplevanidnotesnoteid — not yet observed live.

get.description:
Returns every note category available in the current context as a **bare JSON array** — this endpoint does not use the pagination envelope, and it ignores query parameters such as `$top`.

A category only appears here once it has been opted in to the current context's committee through the Committees picker on its detail page in the VAN UI; being listed on the Note Categories page is not enough. The sandbox committee has none opted in, so only the empty array has been observed live.

Only a category whose `assignableTypes` contain `Person` can be used on a person note; sending any other id to `POST /people/{vanId}/notes` returns 400. See `GET /notes/categoryTypes` for the full vocabulary of `assignableTypes`.

get.description:
Returns the entity types a note category can be assigned to — the vocabulary of `NoteCategory.assignableTypes` — as a **bare JSON array of strings**, with no pagination envelope.

The official docs state that "in almost all cases" the available types are `Event`, `Location`, `Person` and `Organization`, and give `["Person", "Organization", "Event", "Location"]` as the example response. Because a context can in principle expose a different set, this endpoint is the authoritative list for a given context and the schema below does not close the set with an `enum`.

RequestValidationRedirect.description:
The request never reached the API. ASP.NET request validation rejects a path segment containing `<`, `>`, `*` or `&` and hands the request to the VAN web application, which answers **302** with `Location: /Error.aspx?EID={code}` and a small HTML "Object moved" body. Clients that follow the redirect land on the web app's HTML "Oops...something went wrong" page with status 200 — HTML, not JSON, from an endpoint that otherwise only speaks JSON.

Other unusual path characters take different routes: `:` and `"` give the IIS HTML 404, and a backslash gives the standard JSON 404 envelope.

Location.description: The web application's error page, e.g. /Error.aspx?EID=26B226-343EF8

BadRequest.description:
Validation error, as the standard JSON envelope.

Two unrelated cases share this status and answer with `text/html` instead, because the request is rejected in front of the API and never reaches it: a percent-encoded control character such as `%7F` in the path gets IIS's "Bad Request - Invalid URL" page, and `%00` gets Cloudflare's "400 Bad Request" page. Check the content type before parsing.

ServerError.description: Internal server error. The API returns 500 (not 400) for various malformed inputs, e.g. negative delayInMilliseconds on /echoes, non-ASCII filter values on /surveyQuestions, vanId 0 or null phone entries on /people/find, a null phone entry on the person write endpoints, an `identifiers` entry with the valid type `dwid` on POST /people/create, and a negative vanId — in the path or the body — or a secondary equal to the primary on PUT /people/{vanId}/mergeInto. PersonMatchCriteria.description:
Match criteria. Every field is optional in the sense that the API never rejects a sparse body — but matching only happens once the criteria reach one of these minimum combinations:

- firstName + lastName + emails[].email
- firstName + lastName + phones[].phoneNumber
- firstName + lastName + addresses[].zipOrPostalCode (zip5) + dateOfBirth
- firstName + lastName + addresses[].addressLine1 (street number **and** street name) + addresses[].zipOrPostalCode (zip5)
- emails[].email on its own (phones[].phoneNumber on its own also works)

Below that, the request is answered Unmatched without a search rather than rejected. A valid vanId overrides all other criteria and skips the threshold entirely.

x-provenance.note: Combination list from the docs' Match Candidate common model, each combination confirmed against sandbox vanId 102719047 (see the x-provenance on POST /people/find for the full matched/unmatched probe list). `addresses` is absent from the docs' find request example but is accepted and is the only way to supply zip5 or a street address as criteria — name + dob + zip matched, name + dob alone did not.

vanId.description: VAN id of the person; a valid vanId overrides all other criteria and is looked up directly, with no minimum-combination threshold. Warning: the API returns 500 for vanId 0.

firstName.description: Required by every combination except the email-only (or phone-only) one. Compared case- and accent-insensitively, and may match nicknames and variants unless the context has "Disable Partial Matching" enabled. A first name that disagrees with the person record turns an otherwise-matching request into Unmatched.

middleName.description: Never part of a minimum combination; only narrows a match that the other criteria already reached.

lastName.description: Required by every combination except the email-only (or phone-only) one. Same comparison rules as firstName.

dateOfBirth.description: Only reaches the threshold in combination with firstName, lastName and a zip5 in addresses[]. Name + dateOfBirth alone returns Unmatched.

emails.description: Email addresses to match on. The strongest single criterion: an address on its own reaches the threshold, no name required. Compared case-insensitively.

phones.description: Phone numbers to match on. Reaches the threshold with firstName + lastName, and — undocumented but observed — on its own as well. Punctuation is ignored: "907-555-4242" matches a stored "9075554242". A null array entry returns 500.
phones.x-docs-discrepancy: The docs list only an email address as a criterion sufficient on its own; a phone number alone also matched (observed 2026-08-04, sandbox vanId 102719047).

addresses.description: Addresses to match on — the only way to supply the zip5 that two of the minimum combinations require. Never sufficient on its own, and never with a name alone: firstName + lastName + zipOrPostalCode returns Unmatched unless a dateOfBirth or a street address comes with it. A null entry in this array is tolerated (404 Unmatched, not 500).

PersonMatchAddress.description: An address used as match criteria — the fields the matcher reads, unlike the fuller PersonAddressInput used when writing. Only two shapes reach the matching threshold, both alongside firstName and lastName: zipOrPostalCode + dateOfBirth, or addressLine1 + zipOrPostalCode.

x-provenance.note: Accepted by POST /people/find and confirmed to drive matching against sandbox vanId 102719047 (742 Evergreen Terrace, Springfield AK 99501): name+dob+zip and name+addressLine1+zip both matched; name+zip alone, name+"Evergreen Terrace" (no street number)+zip, and name+addressLine1+wrong zip all returned Unmatched. Only these fields were probed as criteria; the write model's other fields (addressLine2/3, type, …) are accepted but were not observed to affect the outcome.

addressLine1.description: Street address. Must carry both the street **number** and the street name to count toward a match: "742 Evergreen Terrace" matched, "Evergreen Terrace" did not.

city.description: City or town. Not part of any minimum combination.

stateOrProvince.description: Two or three character state or province code, e.g. "MN", "ON", "NSW". Not part of any minimum combination.

zipOrPostalCode.description: The zip5 that the date-of-birth and street-address combinations both require. Must agree with the person record — a right street with a wrong zip does not match.

countryCode.description: Two character ISO country code supported by the VAN context. Defaults to the context's country.

PersonMatchEmail.description: An email address used as match criteria — the address only, unlike the fuller PersonEmailInput used when writing.

PersonMatchPhone.description: A phone number used as match criteria — no type or opt-in fields, unlike the PersonPhoneInput used when writing.

Read-only; whether this is the number VAN treats as the person's best. **At most one number per person carries it, across all types — it is not per `phoneType`**, and a person can have several phones and no best one at all. It is also what `GET /people?phoneNumber=` searches, so a person with no best number cannot be found by phone there.

Which number gets it, in order:

1. The number written with `isPreferred: true`, whatever its type or device — including a Work or Fax number that could not otherwise qualify. Writing a new preferred number moves both flags to it.
2. Otherwise the most recently added number among those that qualify — `phoneType` `Personal` with a `deviceType` other than `Fax`. A `Cell` outranks every other device: once a person has one, a later `Landline`, `VoIP` or `Unknown` number does not take the flag, while a newer `Cell` does.
3. If nothing qualifies — every number is `Work`, `Other` or a Personal fax, and none is preferred — **no number is best** and every entry reads `false`.

Recency does decide between equals: a second plain Personal took it from the first, and a second Cell from the first — including two Cells written in the same request, where the later array entry won despite an identical dateCreated, so the tiebreak is insertion order rather than the minute-resolution timestamp. The zero-best case was confirmed on work-only, other-only and Personal/fax-only people, each of whom GET /people?phoneNumber= then failed to find, while a work-only person whose number was written with isPreferred:true was best and was found.

dateAcquired.description: For API-created people this is "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z" (the .NET default date).

emails.description: Null unless the request included $expand=emails; an empty array when expanded and none exist.

phones.description: Null unless the request included $expand=phones; an empty array when expanded and none exist. Every phone on the person is returned, not just the best known one.

addresses.description: Null unless the request included $expand=addresses; an empty array when expanded and none exist. Provides the best known Home address and the best known Mailing address only — the same address appears under both types when it fills both roles, and Work/Custom addresses are omitted.

notes.description: Notes on the person, when requested with `$expand=notes`. Same objects GET /people/{vanId}/notes returns, with two differences: an uncategorized note's `category` is null here rather than the `{"noteCategoryId": 0, "name": null}` stub, and the array is not paginated. View-restricted notes are withheld here too.

x-provenance.note: Compared side by side against GET /people/102714507/notes on a person with six notes: same ids and fields, different `category` rendering and a different item order.
